title: Foundations & Organisational Structure
intro: Where MM sits in SAP S/4HANA, how to find your way around the system, and the organisational units every purchasing and inventory process is built on.
objectives: Explain what SAP S/4HANA is and where MM fits
Navigate the Fiori launchpad and SAP GUI
Define client, company code, plant, storage location, purchasing organisation and purchasing group
Describe how these units are assigned to each other

lessons.title: SAP S/4HANA and where MM fits
lessons.body:
SAP S/4HANA is SAP's current ERP suite. It runs only on SAP's in-memory database, SAP HANA, and replaces the older SAP ECC. ECC mainstream maintenance ends in 2027, which is why so many companies are migrating now. Every migration needs end-user training.

Three ways to run it

  • On-premise: installed on the company's own servers
  • Cloud Private Edition: hosted by SAP, but customisable like on-premise (the C_TS452 exam covers this)
  • Cloud Public Edition: standardised SaaS with less customisation

What MM covers

MM (Materials Management) handles everything about buying and holding goods. In S/4HANA marketing it appears as Sourcing and Procurement plus Inventory Management.

  • Purchasing: requisitions, quotations, purchase orders, contracts
  • Inventory management: goods receipts, issues, transfers, stock
  • Invoice verification: checking supplier invoices against POs and receipts
  • Master data: suppliers, materials, purchasing info records

Integration: MM never works alone

  • FI (Financial Accounting): every goods receipt and invoice creates accounting entries
  • CO (Controlling): purchases charged to cost centres
  • SD (Sales): stock availability for customer orders
  • PP (Production Planning): MRP creates purchase requisitions
  • EWM / QM: warehouse and quality management

Trainer angle: learners always ask “what happens in accounting when I do this?” Knowing the FI link makes you credible.
lessons.narration: Let's start with the big picture. SAP S/4HANA is SAP's current enterprise resource planning suite. It runs on SAP's own in-memory database, called HANA, and it replaces the older system, SAP ECC. Mainstream maintenance for ECC ends in 2027, and that's why so many companies are migrating right now. For you as a trainer, that's good news, because every migration means staff who need training. S/4HANA can run in three ways: on-premise, on the company's own servers; Cloud Private Edition, hosted by SAP but still customisable; and Cloud Public Edition, a standardised software-as-a-service version. The certification you're aiming for covers Private Edition. Now, MM stands for Materials Management. It covers everything to do with buying goods and holding them in stock: purchasing, inventory management, invoice verification, and the master data behind all of it, such as suppliers and materials. The key idea to remember is that MM never works alone. Every goods receipt and every supplier invoice creates entries in Financial Accounting. Purchases can be charged to cost centres in Controlling. Sales checks stock that MM manages. And production planning creates the purchase requisitions that MM turns into orders. When your learners ask what happens in accounting when they post something, you'll have the answer.
keyTerms: Enterprise Resource Planning: one integrated system for the whole business
SAP's in-memory database that S/4HANA runs on
The predecessor ERP system, being replaced by S/4HANA
Materials Management: purchasing, inventory, invoice verification

tryIt.task: Log in to your practice system and note which edition and release it is (look under your user menu → About, or System → Status in SAP GUI).

lessons.title: Finding your way: Fiori launchpad and SAP GUI
lessons.body:
S/4HANA has two user interfaces. Your learners will use one or both, so you need to be fluent in each.

SAP Fiori launchpad

  • Browser-based, works on tablets and phones
  • Apps appear as tiles, organised into spaces and pages
  • Role-based: a purchaser sees purchasing apps, a warehouse clerk sees inventory apps (e.g. business role SAP_BR_PURCHASER)
  • App types: transactional (do something), analytical (KPIs, reports), fact sheets (look something up)
  • Many classic transactions are available as Fiori tiles, often labelled “– Advanced”

SAP GUI

  • The classic desktop client, still widely used
  • Navigation by transaction codes typed in the command field
  • /n + code = open in the same window (e.g. /nME21N); /o + code = open in a new window
  • Configuration lives in the IMG (Implementation Guide), transaction SPRO

Core MM transactions and their Fiori equivalents

ProcessSAP GUIFiori app
Create purchase requisitionME51NManage Purchase Requisitions
Create purchase orderME21NCreate Purchase Order – Advanced / Manage Purchase Orders
Goods receipt / movementMIGOPost Goods Movement
Supplier invoiceMIROCreate Supplier Invoice – Advanced
Supplier masterBPManage Business Partner Master Data
Material masterMM01 / MM02 / MM03Manage Product Master Data

Fiori app names change between releases. Always check the SAP Fiori apps reference library for the release your client uses.
lessons.narration: S/4HANA gives users two ways in. The first is the SAP Fiori launchpad. It runs in a web browser, so it also works on tablets and phones. Applications appear as tiles, grouped into spaces and pages, and what each user sees depends on their business role. A purchaser sees purchasing apps; a warehouse clerk sees inventory apps. Fiori apps come in three flavours: transactional apps, where you actually do something like create an order; analytical apps, which show figures and reports; and fact sheets, which let you look something up quickly. The second interface is the classic SAP GUI. Here you navigate with transaction codes. Type slash N followed by a code to open it in the same window, for example slash N, M E, 2 1, N, to create a purchase order. Type slash O instead to open it in a new window. The configuration of the whole system lives in the Implementation Guide, which you reach with the transaction S P R O. Learn these core codes now, because you'll use them all through the course: M E 5 1 N for purchase requisitions, M E 2 1 N for purchase orders, M I G O for goods movements, M I R O for supplier invoices, B P for business partners, and M M 0 1, 0 2 and 0 3 to create, change and display materials. One last trainer tip: Fiori app names change between releases, so always check the Fiori apps reference library for the release your client is on.
keyTerms: Browser-based, role-based entry point with app tiles
Short code to open a function in SAP GUI, e.g. ME21N
/n opens a transaction in the same window, /o in a new one
Implementation Guide: where the system is configured

tryIt.task: Open the Fiori launchpad and find the apps for purchase requisitions, purchase orders and goods movements. Note their exact names in your system.
In SAP GUI, open ME23N (display purchase order) with /nME23N, then open MIGO in a new window with /oMIGO.
Run SPRO, click 'SAP Reference IMG' and expand Materials Management. Just look — don't change anything.

lessons.title: Enterprise structure: client, company code, plant, storage location
lessons.body:
Every transaction in MM happens somewhere in the organisation. These units are set up once in configuration and almost never change.

Client

  • The highest level: a self-contained system with its own master data and settings
  • 3-digit number (e.g. 100). You choose it when you log on
  • Companies often have separate clients for development, testing, training and production

Company code

  • The smallest unit for which a complete set of accounts (balance sheet, P&L) is produced: in practice, a legal entity
  • 4 characters (e.g. 1010)
  • Defined in FI, but MM depends on it because purchases and stock have a financial value

Plant

  • A logistics location: factory, warehouse, branch, distribution centre
  • 4 characters. Each plant belongs to exactly one company code
  • Stock is usually valued at plant level (the valuation area is normally the plant)
  • Material master data has plant-specific views (e.g. MRP settings per plant)

Storage location

  • A place within a plant where stock is physically kept: raw materials store, finished goods store, spare parts cage
  • 4 characters. Belongs to one plant
  • Stock quantities are managed at storage location level (values at plant level)

The hierarchy

Client → Company code → Plant → Storage location

Common learner confusion: a storage location is not a warehouse bin. Bins belong to warehouse management (EWM), which is a separate, more detailed layer.
lessons.narration: Every MM transaction happens somewhere in the organisation, and SAP models that with organisational units. They're set up once in configuration and rarely change. At the top is the client. A client is a self-contained system with its own data and settings, identified by a three-digit number that you choose when you log on. Companies usually have separate clients for development, testing, training and real production work. Below the client is the company code. This is the smallest unit for which a complete set of accounts can be produced, a balance sheet and a profit and loss statement. In practice, think of it as a legal entity. It's defined by the finance team, but MM depends on it, because everything you buy and store has a financial value. Next comes the plant. A plant is a logistics location, such as a factory, a warehouse or a branch. Each plant belongs to exactly one company code, and stock is normally valued at plant level. Finally, inside each plant you have storage locations. These are the physical places where stock is kept, like a raw materials store or a finished goods store. Stock quantities are tracked by storage location, while stock values are tracked by plant. So the hierarchy is: client, company code, plant, storage location. One classic learner mistake: a storage location is not a warehouse bin. Bins belong to warehouse management, which is a separate and more detailed layer.
keyTerms: Highest org level; self-contained data and settings; 3 digits
Legal entity with its own complete set of accounts; 4 characters
Logistics location; belongs to one company code; usual valuation level
Place within a plant where stock is kept; quantity level
Level at which stock is valued, normally the plant

tryIt.task: Find which client you log on to and write it down.

In SPRO → Enterprise Structure → Definition, display (don't change) the company codes, plants and storage locations in your system. Many SAP Best Practices systems use company code 1010 and plant 1010, but check yours.
Display any material with MM03 and look at the Plant Data / Storage views to see where it is stocked.

lessons.title: Purchasing organisation and purchasing group
lessons.body:
Purchasing organisation

  • The unit that negotiates conditions (prices, terms) with suppliers and is legally responsible for purchasing
  • 4 characters
  • Every purchase order is created for one purchasing organisation
  • Supplier purchasing data (currency, payment terms, incoterms) is maintained per purchasing organisation

Three ways to organise purchasing

  • Centralised (cross-company): one purchasing org buys for plants in several company codes. It is not assigned to a company code
  • Company-specific: one purchasing org per company code, buying for all its plants
  • Plant-specific: one purchasing org per plant

A purchasing org is assigned to the plants it buys for. One plant can be served by several purchasing orgs.

A reference purchasing organisation lets other purchasing orgs use its negotiated contracts and conditions.

Purchasing group

  • A buyer or team of buyers responsible for certain materials or activities
  • 3 characters (e.g. 001)
  • Not assigned to any other organisational unit: it is defined independently
  • Used for responsibility, reporting and as the internal contact on purchase documents

Easy way to remember it: the purchasing organisation is the legal buyer; the purchasing group is the person at the desk.
lessons.narration: Now the two purchasing units. The purchasing organisation is the unit that negotiates prices and terms with suppliers, and it carries the legal responsibility for purchasing. It has a four-character key, and every purchase order belongs to exactly one purchasing organisation. Supplier data such as order currency and payment terms is also stored per purchasing organisation. Companies can organise purchasing in three ways. Centralised, or cross-company: one purchasing organisation buys for plants in several company codes, and in that case it is not assigned to any company code. Company-specific: one purchasing organisation per company code. Or plant-specific: one purchasing organisation per plant. Whatever the model, purchasing organisations are assigned to the plants they buy for, and one plant can be served by several of them. There's also the reference purchasing organisation, which lets other purchasing organisations use its contracts and conditions. Then there's the purchasing group. This is a buyer, or a team of buyers. It has a three-character key, and here's the important point: it isn't assigned to any other organisational unit. It's used to show who is responsible and for reporting. An easy way to remember the difference: the purchasing organisation is the legal buyer, and the purchasing group is the person at the desk.
keyTerms: Negotiates conditions with suppliers; legally responsible; 4 characters
Buyer or team of buyers; not assigned to org units; 3 characters
Purchasing org not assigned to a company code; buys across companies
Its contracts and conditions can be used by other purchasing orgs

tryIt.task: Display the purchasing organisations in your system (SPRO → Enterprise Structure → Definition → Materials Management → Maintain Purchasing Organization, or transaction OX08).
Display the purchasing groups (SPRO → Materials Management → Purchasing → Create Purchasing Groups, or OME4).
Open any purchase order with ME23N and find its purchasing organisation and purchasing group on the Org. Data tab of the header.

lessons.title: Putting it together: assignments
lessons.body:
Organisational units only work once they're assigned to each other. These assignments decide which plants a purchasing org can buy for and which company code pays.

The key assignments

AssignmentRuleTransaction
Plant → company codeEach plant belongs to exactly one company codeOX18
Storage location → plantDefined inside the plantOX09
Purchasing org → company codeOptional (omit for cross-company purchasing)OX01
Purchasing org → plantMany-to-manyOX17
Purchasing groupNo assignmentOME4

Worked example: Azur Industries (fictional)

  • Company code FR01 Azur Industries SAS (France)
  • Plant FR10 Fréjus factory with storage locations RM01 (raw materials) and FG01 (finished goods)
  • Plant FR20 Nice warehouse with storage location WH01
  • Purchasing org FR00 assigned to company code FR01 and to both plants
  • Purchasing groups 001 (raw materials buyer) and 002 (indirect purchases)

A buyer in group 001 creates a PO in purchasing org FR00 for plant FR10, storage location RM01. On goods receipt, stock increases in RM01 (quantity) and in FR10 (value), and the accounting entry posts in company code FR01.

In class, draw this structure on the board before any transaction. Learners make far fewer org-data errors on POs once they've seen the picture.
lessons.narration: Organisational units only work once they're assigned to each other. These assignments decide which plants a purchasing organisation can buy for, and which company code ends up paying. Here are the rules. Each plant is assigned to exactly one company code. Storage locations are defined inside their plant. A purchasing organisation can be assigned to a company code, but that's optional: leave it unassigned and it can buy across companies. Purchasing organisations are assigned to plants, and that relationship is many-to-many. And purchasing groups aren't assigned to anything. Let's make it concrete with a fictional company, Azur Industries. It has one company code, F R 0 1, in France. It has two plants: F R 1 0, a factory in Fréjus, with a raw materials store and a finished goods store, and F R 2 0, a warehouse in Nice. One purchasing organisation, F R 0 0, is assigned to the company code and to both plants. And there are two purchasing groups: 0 0 1 for raw materials and 0 0 2 for indirect purchases. So when a buyer in group 0 0 1 creates a purchase order in purchasing organisation F R 0 0 for the Fréjus plant and the raw materials store, here's what happens at goods receipt: the quantity goes up in the storage location, the value goes up in the plant, and the accounting entry posts in company code F R 0 1. A tip for class: draw this structure on the board before you show a single transaction. Learners make far fewer mistakes with organisational data once they've seen the picture.
keyTerms: Assign purchasing organisation to company code
One purchasing org serves several plants; one plant can have several purchasing orgs

tryIt.task: Display (don't change) OX18, OX01 and OX17 in your system and draw your system's org structure on paper, like the Azur example.
Trainer kit: turn your drawing into a clean one-page diagram. It becomes slide 1 of your sellable module.

quiz.q: Which unit is the smallest for which a complete set of accounts can be drawn up?
quiz.explain: The company code is the legal entity level with its own balance sheet and P&L.

quiz.q: A plant can be assigned to…
options: One client only, with no company code
quiz.explain: Each plant belongs to exactly one company code.
Quantities are held per storage location; values are normally held per plant.

quiz.q: Which statement about purchasing groups is correct?
options: They are assigned to a purchasing organisation
They are assigned to a plant
They are not assigned to other organisational units
They are assigned to a company code
quiz.explain: Purchasing groups (buyers) are defined independently of the other org units.

quiz.q: A purchasing organisation that buys for plants in several company codes is…
options: Assigned to all those company codes
Not assigned to any company code
quiz.explain: Cross-company (centralised) purchasing orgs are not assigned to a company code; they are assigned to the plants.

quiz.q: What is the relationship between purchasing organisations and plants?
quiz.explain: One purchasing org can serve several plants, and one plant can be served by several purchasing orgs.

quiz.q: Which transaction creates a purchase order in SAP GUI?
quiz.explain: ME21N creates POs. ME51N creates purchase requisitions.

quiz.q: In S/4HANA, suppliers are maintained with…
quiz.explain: S/4HANA uses the Business Partner for suppliers; old vendor transactions redirect to BP.

quiz.q: Which edition does the C_TS452 certification cover?
quiz.explain: C_TS452 covers S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition (also relevant for on-premise).

options: Opens MIGO in the same window
Opens MIGO in a new window
quiz.explain: /o opens a new session; /n replaces the current one.
